stories.headline: 'Built that way': KNCB's news director on why the Spanish water warning came 12 hours late
stories.dek: A state snapshot notes delays in Spanish-language alerts but puts no number on them. Marisol Fuentes-Vega has the number, and an explanation.
body: Marisol Fuentes-Vega keeps the log open on her desk at KNCB. It shows the minute the station's fax line printed the city's boil-water notice for Districts 3 and 4: 6:03 a.m. on Monday, Sept. 27. The English alert had gone out at 5:30 the evening before.

"Twelve hours and thirty-three minutes," said Fuentes-Vega, the station's news director. "I have read that line so many times I could say it in my sleep. For twelve hours, the people who listen to us were filling glasses from the tap."

On Tuesday the Texas Division of Emergency Management released its first after-action snapshot of public communications during Hurricane Rafael. The document notes "observed delays in Spanish-language alert distribution." It does not say how long the delays were, and it makes no recommendations.

The same day, a local chapter of the League of United Latin American Citizens filed a complaint with the state, citing its limited-English-proficiency plan and Title VI of the Civil Rights Act. KNCB read the complaint on the air.

In an interview with Coastline Public Radio, Fuentes-Vega described what she says is a structural problem, not a one-night failure. English alerts, she said, move automatically from the agency that writes them to phones, television and radio. Spanish versions wait for a translation, and the translation waits for a person.

"Nobody decided that Spanish speakers should find out last," she said. "It is built that way. The English goes out at the speed of a computer. The Spanish goes out at the speed of whoever is still in the office."

KNCB is the main news source for an estimated 34,000 Spanish-speaking listeners in Corpus Christi. During the storm the station stayed on the air on generator power for as long as its transmitter held, translating warnings itself as they arrived.

Cassandra Trejo-Morales, a spokesperson for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management, has said the Spanish notice was delayed and has attributed the delay to limits in the county's language-access service. The county has not yet said what it will change.
Fuentes-Vega said she is not waiting. The station now calls the city and the county every evening to ask whether anything has been issued in English that has not reached it in Spanish.
"It should not depend on us remembering to call," she said. "But until it doesn't, we call."

The state snapshot is a first look; a fuller review is expected later. Fuentes-Vega said she plans to ask county commissioners to require that every emergency notice go out in both languages at the same time.
